processes.summary: A live process/session list with auto-refresh, filtering and one-click kill. MySQL uses SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST; PostgreSQL uses pg_stat_activity. Long-running rows are tinted so runaway or blocking work stands out before you stop it.
processes.howToOpen: Activity menu -> Processes (also on the native Tools menu)
keyActions: Filter rows across all cells
Set the auto-refresh interval (1/2/3/5/10/30s)
Pause/Resume and manual Refresh
Set the long-query threshold and toggle 'only long' / sort longest-first
Select a row and 'Kill query' (KILL QUERY / pg_cancel_backend) or 'Kill connection' (KILL / pg_terminate_backend)
Open Thread progress for a selected MySQL/PostgreSQL/SQL Server backend
Copy/Export the current grid
processes.engines: MySQL, PostgreSQL, Redis and ClickHouse (the processList capability). Kill uses MySQL/PG semantics; killing another backend needs SUPER/CONNECTION_ADMIN (MySQL) or pg_signal_backend (PostgreSQL) or the button is disabled with the missing-privilege tip.
processes.caveats: Requires a live connection. Interactive kill can be turned off in Settings -> Safety, which makes the panel a read-only monitor. Killing others is privilege-gated and shown greyed when blocked.

replication.summary: A replication dashboard refreshed every 5 seconds. MySQL summarizes every channel and exposes stopped-channel errors; PostgreSQL adds logical-replication SQL helpers. Use it to see whether replication is healthy and why it stalled.
replication.howToOpen: Activity menu -> Replication (also on the native Tools menu)
keyActions: View per-channel health summary; click a channel row to expand full detail
Toggle 'all fields' for the complete field dump
Pause/Resume the 5s poll and manual Refresh
PostgreSQL only: generate CREATE/DROP publication, CREATE logical/drop replication slot, and CREATE/REFRESH/DROP subscription SQL (emitted into the editor for review, never run)
replication.engines: MySQL and PostgreSQL (the sqlDba capability). Monitoring works on both; the logical-replication action buttons appear only on PostgreSQL.
replication.caveats: Requires a live connection. The PG action buttons only generate SQL into the editor; they do not execute. Read-only monitoring otherwise.

dbaviews.summary: A categorized catalog of read-only health queries over each engine's system views. Results appear in a sortable grid. Disabled instrumentation is diagnosed with copyable fix SQL instead of looking like an empty result.
dbaviews.howToOpen: Server menu -> DBA views (also on the native Tools menu)
keyActions: Pick a view from the categorized list (demanding views carry a warning badge; privilege-blocked ones are locked with the missing grant named)
Set a row limit (100/1000/10000/unlimited)
Optional auto-refresh (Off/5s/10s/30s)
Cancel or hard-Kill a slow view query
Copy/Export the grid
MySQL 'Scheduled events' view: emit scheduler on/off and per-event ENABLE/DISABLE SQL into the editor (review-only)
dbaviews.engines: All engines that ship a view set: MySQL/MariaDB/Percona, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse and Redis each have curated views (the panel itself has no engine gate).
dbaviews.caveats: Requires a live connection. The available view set depends on engine and server flavour; some views need a monitoring role/extension and are shown blocked. The event-management actions only generate SQL.

tuner.summary: A read-only health analyzer with a 0–100 score, category sub-scores, end-of-life status and guided findings. Fixes are copied or inserted into the editor for review, never executed by the panel.
tuner.howToOpen: Server menu -> Tuner (labelled 'Server tuner'; also on the native Tools menu)
keyActions: Run analysis / Re-analyze
Filter All vs Problems (advice+warnings+critical)
Expand a finding for detail and recommendation
Copy a guided fix, 'Copy all', or insert the fix script into the editor (never run)
Export the report as Markdown
tuner.engines: Gated to the tuner capability (MySQL, PostgreSQL, Redis, ClickHouse, SQLite). The panel has explicit rule sets and copy for MySQL family, PostgreSQL and Redis; on engines the backend does not yet support, tuner_analyze returns a 'not supported yet' notice.
tuner.caveats: Requires a live connection. Reads status/variables only (safe on prod). Which engines actually return a report depends on the backend tuner_analyze support, which cannot be verified without a live server.

routines.summary: Create and edit procedures, functions, triggers and events with structured metadata and a full SQL body editor. Review exact DDL before saving. MySQL preserves the original routine if replacement fails.
routines.howToOpen: Schema menu -> Routines (also on the native Tools menu); can also be opened on a specific routine from the schema tree
keyActions: Filter and pick a routine, or create a new procedure/function/trigger/event with the + buttons
Edit name, returns/params, trigger timing/events/table/level/when/function (PG), event schedule
Show DDL / Copy DDL; Revert; Create/Save
Execute... builds a CALL/SELECT from a typed form (inserted into the editor, not run)
PostgreSQL procedures/functions: step-through Debug
routines.engines: MySQL and PostgreSQL (the sqlDba capability). PostgreSQL has no scheduled events (the + event button is hidden) and its triggers use the function-calling form.
routines.caveats: Requires a live connection. Read-only on prod-tagged and read-only connections (editing disabled with a banner). Debug executes the routine body (rolled back) so it is blocked on prod/read-only.

txshell.summary: A keyboard-driven SQL console with real result grids, pipelines, variables, file sources, fan-out, command substitution and typed result diffs. Use it to query, compare, export and script without leaving the app.
txshell.howToOpen: SQL menu -> TxShell (also on the native Tools menu)
keyActions: Run SQL directly; pipe rows with |> to stages and sinks (grid, chart, to <format>, save/append <file>, insert into <table> [@dest])
diff #42 [key id ...] compares the pipeline input with an explicitly selected captured result, aligning columns by name and emitting typed change rows
$(...) executes a nested TxShell command or file pipeline (never the OS shell): one cell becomes a scalar, larger results deterministic TSV
Meta commands: \help, \clear, \vars, \unset, \history, \timing, \l, \dt, \dv, \df, \d, \source <file>, \edit, plus psql catalog metas
$name = value variables; !line runs your OS shell; @pattern SQL fans out read-only across matching connections
from <file> loads a CSV/TSV/JSON file as a result set; Tab-complete, up/down history, Shift-Enter for newline, Clear
txshell.engines: All SQL engines (the sql capability: MySQL, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, SQLite, Parquet). Not Redis.
txshell.caveats: Statements are audited with redaction. Fan-out is read-only and confirms wide/prod matches. Cross-server insert needs an open destination. Substitution and result diffs have explicit limits and shape checks.

find.summary: Three search scopes in one panel: Usages finds database references, In database searches table values, and In files searches local SQL scripts. Use it before destructive refactors, during incidents, or to find migration code.
find.howToOpen: Find & Compare menu -> Find (also on the native Tools menu), then the Usages / In database / In files tabs. Open buffers are passed to the Usages scope so unsaved scripts are searched too; a programmatic open can preselect the scope.
keyActions: Switch scope with the Usages / In database / In files tabs; a scope the engine cannot serve is greyed with the reason on hover
Usages: pick a schema, table, and optionally a column; Find; filter by confidence (everything / likely and certain / certain only)
In database: type a value; choose match mode (contains/exact/starts with), case sensitivity, numbers & dates opt-in, rows-per-table cap; Search / Stop; open a hit's table in the data browser
In files: choose a folder (defaults to the current file's directory), enter text, set extensions and case sensitivity; click a hit to open the file at that line
find.engines: In files works on every engine, including offline - it never touches the server. Usages and In database need the findUsages / dbSearch capabilities (MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server); on other engines those two tabs are greyed with the reason, never hidden.
find.caveats: Usages and In database need a live connection and are read-only. Usages covers only the selected schema, not application code. In database skips binary columns and reports skipped/truncated work so absence is not misread. In files flags capped results partial.

colprofile.summary: Profile actual column values: rows, NULLs, distinct counts, selectivity, min/max/avg and lengths. Large tables are sampled with the sample size shown. Unlike Analyze, this reports the data rather than optimizer statistics.
colprofile.howToOpen: Data menu -> Column profile (also on the native Tools menu)
keyActions: Pick a schema and table, then Profile
'Read all rows' to switch from a sample to a full scan
Per-column 'top' shows the most common values in a modal
Reads a row estimate first so huge tables are sampled rather than scanned blind
colprofile.engines: MySQL and PostgreSQL (the sqlDba capability); non-postgres engines are treated as MySQL.
colprofile.caveats: Requires a live connection. Sampled figures are labelled as such (distinct counts in particular run low on a sample); a banner warns when numbers come from a sample.

sequences.summary: Create, alter, restart and drop sequence objects without drop-and-recreate. Review the exact ALTER/CREATE statements before applying them and read the current position before a restart.
sequences.howToOpen: Schema menu -> Sequences (also on the native Tools menu); can be opened on a specific sequence from the schema tree
keyActions: Pick a schema and sequence, or New
Edit name, type (PG), start/increment/min/max/cache and cycle
See current position; Restart to a typed value (with a warning)
Copy the generated SQL, Apply/Create, or Drop
sequences.engines: PostgreSQL and MariaDB (the panel resolves the engine itself). Gated to the sqlDba capability (MySQL/PostgreSQL); on plain MySQL it shows a message that MySQL has no sequence object (AUTO_INCREMENT is the nearest equivalent).
sequences.caveats: Requires a live connection. Applies changes directly via execute_query (not just a preview). MariaDB stores a maximum one lower than given, so values are re-read after apply.

types.summary: Edit PostgreSQL composite types, enums and domains through kind-specific forms. Review DDL before applying it. Enum values cannot be dropped, so removal produces a warning and non-executable marker.
types.howToOpen: Schema menu -> Types (also on the native Tools menu); can be opened on a specific type from the schema tree
keyActions: Pick a schema and type, or start a new composite / enum / domain
Edit attributes/values/checks; see the type signature
Copy the SQL or Insert into editor; Apply/Create (runnable changes only); Drop
types.engines: PostgreSQL only. On other engines it shows a message that composite types/enums/domains are PostgreSQL objects.
types.caveats: Requires a live connection. Apply runs the DDL directly. Enum value removal is deliberately non-executable (commented) with a warning; renames become ALTER ... RENAME and additions ALTER ... ADD.

views.summary: Create, replace, refresh and drop views or materialized views in a full SQL editor. Existing definitions are loaded from the catalog and the exact statements are shown before Apply.
views.howToOpen: Schema menu -> Views (also on the native Tools menu); can be opened on a specific view from the schema tree
keyActions: Pick a schema and view, or + View / + Matview
Edit the SELECT body; PG matview: 'Populate now (WITH DATA)'; ClickHouse matview: choose TO target table or inline ENGINE/ORDER BY/PARTITION BY/POPULATE
PostgreSQL matview: Refresh (optionally CONCURRENTLY)
Copy SQL / Insert into editor / Apply/Create / Drop
views.engines: All SQL engines (the sql capability: MySQL, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, SQLite). Materialized views are editable on PostgreSQL and ClickHouse; only PostgreSQL's is refreshed in place. Redis/Parquet show a message that there are no views to edit.
views.caveats: Requires a live connection. Apply runs the DDL directly. ClickHouse materialized-view storage clauses are best-effort parsed back on load.

dictionary.summary: Create, replace and drop ClickHouse dictionaries with forms for attributes, keys, source, layout and lifetime. A raw-SQL mode covers exotic definitions; every change is shown before Apply.
dictionary.howToOpen: Schema menu -> Dictionary (also on the native Tools menu); can be opened on a specific dictionary from the schema tree
keyActions: Pick a schema and dictionary, or + Dictionary
Edit attributes, primary key, source fields, layout and lifetime; or toggle 'Edit as raw SQL' for the whole CREATE DICTIONARY
Copy SQL / Insert into editor / Apply/Create / Drop
dictionary.engines: ClickHouse only. On other engines it shows a message that a dictionary is a ClickHouse object.
dictionary.caveats: Requires a live connection. Apply runs the DDL directly. A dictionary needs a name, at least one attribute and a primary key to be buildable; non-standard sources are passed through as free text via CUSTOM.

designer.summary: Design table changes as a draft, then review the change set, risk labels and SQL before Apply. Columns, generated expressions, indexes, primary keys, storage engine and partitions are covered.
designer.howToOpen: Schema menu -> Table designer (also on the native Tools menu); can be opened on an existing table from the schema tree
keyActions: Design a new table or edit an existing one (name, MySQL storage engine, MariaDB system-versioning / OR REPLACE)
Add/edit/remove columns (type, nullable, default, generated expr + STORED/VIRTUAL, PK) and secondary indexes (unique, invisible)
MySQL partitions: add / drop / reorganize RANGE partitions; PostgreSQL declarative partitions: create / attach / detach
Review the labelled change set and SQL; Copy to editor; Apply (typed confirm word required for destructive changes or prod)
designer.engines: MySQL/MariaDB and PostgreSQL in practice (engine resolves to postgres or mysql; the menu has no engine gate and the designer is expected to refuse gracefully on engines it cannot serve).
designer.caveats: Requires a live connection. Apply runs statements one at a time (drops last) and goes through server-side production guards; destructive DDL on a prod connection needs the connection unlocked plus the typed word PRODUCTION. On non-SQL/embedded engines the catalog reads would not work; not verifiable without a live server.

compare.summary: Four comparison modes: Schema, Data, Results and Scripts. Compare live catalogs or table rows, existing result grids, or local SQL text. Generated migration and reconciliation scripts always require review.
compare.howToOpen: Find & Compare menu -> Compare (also on the native Tools menu), then the Schema / Data / Results / Scripts tabs. The top bar's Compare icon opens the Schema mode directly as an app-level utility view; a programmatic open can preselect the mode.
keyActions: Switch mode with the Schema / Data / Results / Scripts tabs; a mode the engine cannot serve is greyed with the reason on hover
Schema: pick left and right connection + schema (same engine both sides); Compare; click an entry for its DDL diff; export the report or a reviewed migration script
Data: choose source and target connection/schema/table, pick the key columns; Compare; toggle Insert/Update/Delete (delete off by default); copy the script or Apply after the typed confirm word
Results: pick Result A and Result B from the open result tabs, choose the match columns; Compare
Scripts: Load left/right from a file or paste in place; Swap flips the two sides
compare.engines: Schema compares saved MySQL / PostgreSQL connections (both sides the same engine) regardless of the session in front of you. Data needs the dataCompare capability (MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server); on other engines that tab is greyed with the reason, never hidden. Results and Scripts work on every engine, including offline.
compare.caveats: Schema and Data need live connections; Results needs two result tabs. Data refuses truncated comparisons. Apply writes to the target and deletes are irreversible. Results is a report; Scripts only diffs local text.

pglisten.summary: Watch PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY channels in real time over a dedicated streaming connection. Keep the latest 500 notifications and send a test NOTIFY to prove the round trip.
pglisten.howToOpen: Activity menu -> Listen / Notify (also on the native Tools menu)
keyActions: Enter one or more channel names and press Listen; Stop to release the connection
See connection state (idle/connecting/live/closed)
While live, send a test NOTIFY payload to the first channel to prove the round trip
Clear the received list
pglisten.engines: PostgreSQL only. On other engines it says LISTEN/NOTIFY is a PostgreSQL feature.
pglisten.caveats: Requires a live PostgreSQL connection. The listener holds a dedicated (non-pooled) connection and is stopped on Stop and on unmount to avoid a leak. Only the most recent 500 notifications are kept - it is a live view, not a log.
